title: Unpaid household work is a large economic system that converts time into care, household maintenance, and labor-market capacity
source_unit: U.S. Government Accountability Office, Unpaid Household Work: Estimated Value and Time Spent on Domestic Tasks and Caregiving, GAO-26-107871
geography: United States; analysis of 2021–2024 American Time Use Survey data for individuals age 15 and older, with 2024 national valuation estimates

denominator.unit: U.S. civilian noninstitutionalized population age 15 and older; four years of ATUS diary data pooled

any_unpaid_work.unit: percent performing at least one type of unpaid household work on a typical day, excluding secondary child care

hours_unpaid_work.unit: average hours per day among the full population, excluding secondary child care

including_secondary_childcare.unit: average hours per day when secondary child care is included

mechanism.value: Household functioning depends on a large daily time system that is mostly outside national income and standard employment measures

observations.method: GAO analysis of pooled 2021–2024 American Time Use Survey diary data, with estimates and stated margins of error.
observations.uncertainty: ATUS records a selected diary day rather than a full longitudinal care history; pooled estimates are descriptive and secondary child care can overlap with other activities.
observations.subgroup: U.S. individuals age 15 and older, with separate analysis by sex, age, employment, marital status, family income, and caregiving type.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some unpaid household work is discretionary, reciprocal, or personally meaningful rather than a pure burden; monetary replacement values do not measure subjective welfare or relationship quality.

denominator.unit: U.S. individuals age 15 and older on a typical diary day; caregiving estimates are conditional among people performing each activity

childcare.unit: percent providing primary or secondary child care on a typical day

childcare_hours.unit: average hours per day among people providing child care

adult_care.unit: percent caring for adults on a typical day

sandwich_care.unit: percent caring for adults and children on the same day when secondary child care is included

sandwich_care_hours.unit: average hours per day among people providing sandwich care when secondary child care is included

mechanism.value: Care intensity is concentrated in overlapping life-course roles, creating a time constraint that cannot be inferred from employment status alone

observations.method: GAO analysis of pooled ATUS diary data, with primary and secondary child care, adult care, and same-day sandwich care distinguished.
observations.uncertainty: Care categories overlap; conditional hours among caregivers should not be multiplied by the population share without preserving the denominator distinction, and the sandwich-care estimate has a wider margin of error.
observations.subgroup: People caring for children, adults, or both; age, employment, marital status, sex, and income comparisons are reported where statistically supported.
observations.counterinterpretation: Secondary child care may occur alongside other activities and does not always represent continuous intensive supervision; the same care can provide relational value as well as constraint.

observations.period: 2024 valuation; national market value of unpaid household work

denominator.unit: United States annual national estimate in 2024 dollars

value_excluding_secondary_childcare_low.unit: trillion US dollars estimated annual market value, excluding secondary child care

value_excluding_secondary_childcare_high.unit: trillion US dollars estimated annual market value, excluding secondary child care

value_including_secondary_childcare.unit: trillion US dollars estimated annual market value when secondary child care is included

mechanism.value: The economic system relies on a large unpriced production sector whose visibility changes how policy, taxes, employment, and gender inequality are interpreted

observations.method: GAO replacement-wage valuation using ATUS time estimates and low/high wage assumptions; the report distinguishes replacement-wage and opportunity-cost approaches.
observations.uncertainty: The value is an imputed market-equivalent estimate, not income received or welfare created; results vary with wage assumptions, quality adjustments, and inclusion of secondary child care.
observations.subgroup: National U.S. household-work system, with components separately valued for domestic tasks, caregiving, helping adults, and sandwich care.
observations.counterinterpretation: Market replacement cost can overstate what households would purchase externally and understate relational, cultural, or autonomy value that is not priced in labor markets.

denominator.unit: U.S. individuals age 15 and older analyzed by demographic and employment groups

women_share_unpaid_work.unit: percent of people engaged in unpaid household work, compared with 51.2 percent of the U.S. population

nonemployed_domestic_time_gap.unit: approximately additional hour per day spent on domestic tasks by nonemployed versus employed people

lowest_highest_income_domestic_gap.unit: additional hours per day, or about 20 minutes, among lowest-income versus highest-income groups for domestic tasks

adult_care_gender_pattern.value: Women and men who cared for adults spent similar amounts of time, while nonemployed, older, and lower-income caregivers generally spent more

mechanism.value: Unpaid work is broadly distributed, but the ability to absorb it through paid work, money, or services is unequally distributed

observations.method: GAO subgroup comparisons using pooled ATUS diary estimates, statistical significance tests, and minimum practical-difference thresholds.
observations.uncertainty: The report describes time allocation differences rather than causal effects of income, employment, gender, or marital status; subgroup estimates have stated margins of error.
observations.subgroup: Women and men, married and unmarried people, employed and nonemployed people, age groups, and family-income groups.
observations.counterinterpretation: Similar average time in a category can hide differences in intensity, flexibility, task quality, control, or whether the care is shared or supported by others.

related_sources.claim: Underlying Bureau of Labor Statistics American Time Use Survey 2025 release and definitions.
Related national-accounting context for household production and satellite-account valuation.

boundary: This record adds a U.S. route from unpaid domestic work and caregiving through time scarcity, household production, gender and employment exposure, economic valuation, and policy visibility. It is a secondary analysis of pooled ATUS diary data and imputed market values, not respondent-level longitudinal analysis, causal evidence, a measure of money received, or proof that paid substitution would reproduce household welfare.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official GAO-26-107871 report page reviewed for pooled 2021–2024 ATUS methods, unpaid-work prevalence and hours, caregiving and sandwich-care estimates, subgroup comparisons, valuation assumptions, and 2024 national value ranges.
